The phase portrait for a system of linear differential equations whose matrix has two real, distinct eigenvalues is shown above.
The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_1 = [-1, \ 1]^T$ and $\mathbf{v}_2 = [1, \ 0]^T,$ respectively. 

Identify the relations between $\lambda_1,$ $\lambda_2,$ and $0.$

The straight-line solutions of the system have the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/7282a63a66c9f449844292764e4e7b6f1ec472a47ff18aa7fd0c68dbe6042dbe.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/9bff79e13c06645253e57b8e6f43689c7ce21ac818c3ffdc677e03b5a9b08eb7.png) has the equation 

$$
y= -x,

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/d241239c6475fbcf9559c2fcbbb8ca2805a6692fd1a9b3966fe8b38441075a4d.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form

must approach infinity as $t \to \infty.$ So, we must have $\lambda_1 >  0.$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/b06ebf2f3fa8f0616092292e746e84c7e925c42d38cf1c31dc4f6edede6d001b.png) has the equation 

$$
y= 0,
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/fb40117d63e76b2b2db59313b173b04a9a23ef2a28493a5041584e4c7c60c67d.png)

The tangents along this line are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/44c8b9978f9c0db5fc39702755042f1887a95fb2034bb6b01dd8d025b589aba5.png)
must approach infinity as $t \to \infty.$ So, we must have $\lambda_2 > 0.$

So, for this particular system, both eigenvalues are positive. The dominant eigenvalue is the one with the greatest magnitude.

Now, since the solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ as they move away from the origin, the dominant eigenvalue is $\lambda_2.$

Therefore, $\lambda_2 > \lambda_1 > 0.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f1335e5420fe6e475cded1092e9b1ba621e0d88f46110b69ffef5e35ed080d6e.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=2x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/a53bb4e6cd7552b92424b168d0cda90fa1085b5e72fbf8a3c37a3a948bdcf9ad.png)

decision.explanation: The eigenvalues give factors e^{-t} and e^{2t}; the eigenvectors give lines y=−x and y=2x. The first factor tends to zero, while the second tends to infinity, so nonzero solutions in the respective families approach the origin and escape to infinity. The zero solution remains at the origin. The final diagram includes solution trajectories, making it a phase portrait.

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}\cdot {{field-1}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}\cdot {{field-2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.

observation.name: Question 1
observation.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are ${v}_{1}=[1,\text{ }-1]^{T}$ and ${v}_{2}=[1,\text{ }2]^{T},$ respectively. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}\cdot {{field-1}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}\cdot {{field-2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y={{field-3}}
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line.

decision.explanation: Eigenvalues −1 and 2 give exponential factors e^{-t} and e^{2t}. The vector (1,−1) has slope −1, so its line is y=−x. Since e^{-t} tends to 0 as t tends to infinity, both coordinates of c₁e^{-t}(1,−1) tend to 0, so these solutions approach the origin.

decision.explanation: Each eigenvector has factor e^{λt}, giving e^{-t} and e^{2t}. The eigenvectors (1,−1) and (1,2) determine lines y=−x and y=2x. Since e^{-t} tends to 0, the first family approaches the origin.

observation.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f1335e5420fe6e475cded1092e9b1ba621e0d88f46110b69ffef5e35ed080d6e.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=2x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/a53bb4e6cd7552b92424b168d0cda90fa1085b5e72fbf8a3c37a3a948bdcf9ad.png)

after.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f1335e5420fe6e475cded1092e9b1ba621e0d88f46110b69ffef5e35ed080d6e.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=2x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/a53bb4e6cd7552b92424b168d0cda90fa1085b5e72fbf8a3c37a3a948bdcf9ad.png)

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}\cdot {{field-1}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}\cdot {{field-2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$
y={{field-3}}

${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$

content.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f1335e5420fe6e475cded1092e9b1ba621e0d88f46110b69ffef5e35ed080d6e.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=2x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/a53bb4e6cd7552b92424b168d0cda90fa1085b5e72fbf8a3c37a3a948bdcf9ad.png)

The $\text{phase portrait}$ of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/6a4c15275ba80d01a90b2e010ed95e95f9a75cfa13f8e51db3433f6356949057.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}<0
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ is the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue).

Since the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move towards the origin.

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f838a055e525a264bf36b8e0478d186fe17753bba8c0088fea01ac7c5c1f8d7a.png)

The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/6a4c15275ba80d01a90b2e010ed95e95f9a75cfa13f8e51db3433f6356949057.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}<0
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ is the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue).

Since the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move towards the origin.

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f838a055e525a264bf36b8e0478d186fe17753bba8c0088fea01ac7c5c1f8d7a.png)

The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/44d0f3d13ca03a0644b2f28df9200cd521b7b44d625f346e981d2a54165284f5.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=0
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/6a4c15275ba80d01a90b2e010ed95e95f9a75cfa13f8e51db3433f6356949057.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}<0
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ is the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue).

content.worked_solution:
The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=-x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/44d0f3d13ca03a0644b2f28df9200cd521b7b44d625f346e981d2a54165284f5.png)

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y=0
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/6a4c15275ba80d01a90b2e010ed95e95f9a75cfa13f8e51db3433f6356949057.png)

For this particular system, we have

$$
{\lambda }_{2}<{\lambda }_{1}<0
$$

thus, ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ is the eigenvalue that determines the long-term behavior (dominant eigenvalue).

Since the dominant eigenvalue is ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ solutions become parallel to the straight-line solution containing the vector ${v}_{1}$ as they move towards the origin.

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069584/assets/f838a055e525a264bf36b8e0478d186fe17753bba8c0088fea01ac7c5c1f8d7a.png)

decision.explanation: The vector (2,1) gives slope 1/2, so the line is y=x/2. Its arrows point away from the origin on both sides, implying nonzero solutions grow without bound as t→∞. Therefore λ₁>0; the zero solution remains at the origin.
